newsitem.title: UK: Britain's Clarke stays mute on tax cut.
newsitem.headline: Britain's Clarke stays mute on tax cut.

text.p: Britain's finance minister prepared on Thursday to face ruling Conservative Party critics who say his pro-Europe stance and reluctance to slash taxes are blocking the way to electoral success.

But aides to Chancellor of the Exchequer Kenneth Clarke said his keynote speech to the party's annual conference would disappoint delegates hoping for clear hints of tax cuts in next month's crucial pre-election budget.

Party managers are worried that the debate to which Clarke replies could be the occasion for another display of disunity which would play into the hands of the resurgent opposition Labour Party, currently 20 points ahead in the opinion polls.

His many Conservative critics believe his support for a single European currency is stopping Prime Minister John Major from what they say would be the hugely popular path of ruling out British participation.
They are nervous that the budget Clarke announces at the end of next month will prove a damp squib with voters expecting a tax cutting bonanza.
Clarke was quoted recently as saying that it was "not the case that my budget requires tax cuts in order to win the election".
But his aides said Clarke planned to be mute over taxes unlike last year when he gave the conference a clear hint that he would be able to produce a voter-pleasing budget.
"There will be some news tomorrow, but it doesn't relate to the single currency or to the budget," one said.
The conference has already seen attacks by members of the party's Eurosceptic wing at Major's wait-and-see attitude towards the single currency.
But political observers said the criticisms appear to have been toned down in view of the imminence of the election, and critics of Clarke may similarly pull their punches.

On Wednesday Major told delegates it was essential to maintain Britain's influence in negotiations on how the new money would work even if Britain did not eventually join, and he would not give that up for electoral advantage.

Clarke is set to back this line, following the agreed policy of the cabinet that Britain should wait until late next year before deciding whether it is in Britain's interests to jettison the pound sterling.
Major warned that unless a single currency was carefully crafted following strict economic criteria, it could collapse with catastrophic effects for the whole of Europe.

"This is an issue that if it were to go wrong would crack wide open the European Union," Major told delegates during an impromptu question and answer session. "If it cracked it would impact on this country as well."
Major went on to appeal for the party to end its internal divisions and concentrate its fire on Labour.
He said it was time "this party stopped conducting an internal debate with itself and started conducting a debate with the electorate and the Labour party".
Eurosceptic former Chancellor of the Exchequer Norman Lamont appealed on Wednesday for the intra-party conflict to be buried at least in the run up to the election.
"It's time to unite and it's time to emphasise what makes us different and distinctive on Europe from the Labour party," he told a radio interviewer.
